Context: `PushQueuedCheckpointRefs` was flushing the checkpoint-ref push queue with no OPF (OpenAI Privacy Filter) gate, so with OPF enabled, `entire doctor migrate`'s opt-in "push now" shipped 8-layer (regex-only) content to the remote, untagged, without the OPF decision ever being resolved. The diff adds the same gate the pre-push path has, by extracting `opfGateForCheckpointRefs` (error-returning) from the old `runOPFForCheckpointRefs` (bool-returning).

YOUR ANGLE — ALTITUDE ONLY. Is this fix at the right depth, or is it a bandaid that will be re-broken by the next caller?
- The fix adds the gate at each CALL SITE of `flushCheckpointRefsQueue` (there are two). A deeper fix would put the gate INSIDE `flushCheckpointRefsQueue` — the single chokepoint every flush must pass — so a future third caller cannot forget it. Evaluate that alternative seriously: read `flushCheckpointRefsQueue` and both callers, and say whether moving the gate inside is feasible, what it would cost (e.g. the two callers need opposite failure behaviour — pre-push must never block the user's git push, the migrate path must surface an error), and whether a variant (e.g. the gate inside, plus a policy/flag parameter saying how to fail) would be better than two call-site checks. Give a clear recommendation, not a survey.
- Same question one level up: is there a single chokepoint where checkpoint data leaves the machine (e.g. `batchPushRefs`, `pushRefIfNeeded`, or a push-destination helper) at which "nothing un-OPF'd may leave" could be enforced structurally for BOTH the git-refs and git-branch (entire/checkpoints/v1) backends, rather than per-backend? Check `manual_commit_opf_rewrite.go` for the v1 half.
- Is there an existing guard-test convention in this repo that would enforce the invariant mechanically instead of by review? The repo has precedent for this: grep for guard tests like `TestGitStatusCallSitesPassNoOptionalLocks`, `TestRootBasesAreTrusted`, `TestEntireDirCheckExemptions` — these fail the build when a new call site omits a required flag or an exemption goes unlisted. Assess whether an analogous guard test (every `flushCheckpointRefsQueue` caller passes through the OPF gate) is warranted and practical here, and sketch how it would be written.
- Whether the two callers' asymmetric failure behaviour is expressed at the right level, or whether it is implicit knowledge a future reader must reconstruct.

For each finding report: file, line, a one-line summary, and a concrete recommendation with its tradeoff. Prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding special cases. Be decisive. Do not report correctness bugs or style nits. At most 5 findings, ranked by importance.

    51	func (s *ManualCommitStrategy) prePush(ctx context.Context, remote string, protectFirstUserBranch bool) error {
    52		// This runs inside the user's `git push` pre-push hook. Every checkpoint
    53		// git subprocess spawned here (metadata fetch, policy sync, checkpoint
    54		// push and its recovery fetch) must fail fast rather than block on an
    55		// interactive SSH passphrase prompt — there is no way to answer it here and
    56		// it would hang the user's push. Foreground commands do not set this.
    57		//
    58		// BatchMode=yes suppresses passphrase/PIN prompts (including FIDO2
    59		// verify-required PIN entry). Touch-only security keys still work because
    60		// user-presence touch is not a terminal read. Users who need a PIN prompt
    61		// in this path should load the key into ssh-agent, or set an explicit
    62		// BatchMode=no via GIT_SSH_COMMAND / core.sshCommand (respected by the
    63		// non-interactive SSH helper).
    64		ctx = checkpointremote.WithNonInteractiveSSH(ctx)
    65	
    66		// Load settings once for remote resolution and push_sessions check.
    67		// Spanned because checkpoint-remote resolution can perform a one-time
    68		// network fetch of the metadata branch (fetchMetadataBranchIfMissing),
    69		// which is otherwise invisible in the pre-push trace.
    70		resolveCtx, resolveSpan := perf.Start(ctx, "resolve_push_settings")
    71		ps := resolvePushSettings(resolveCtx, remote)
    72		resolveSpan.End()
    73	
    74		if ps.pushDisabled {
    75			return nil
    76		}
    77	
    78		// Single-remote gate (ENT-1451): checkpoint data syncs only to the
    79		// elected checkpoint sync remote. A dedicated checkpoint_remote URL is
    80		// exempt — it is a dedicated metadata store addressed directly, not a
    81		// remote selected by this push. The gate must stay BELOW
    82		// resolvePushSettings: hasCheckpointURL is only known after resolution,
    83		// so hoisting the gate above it would break the exemption.
    84		//
    85		// Capture is two-phase, straddling this whole function. The proposal runs
    86		// before the gate so that the push which elects a remote by evidence (push
    87		// target agrees with the branch's declared push destination) is also the
    88		// first push to carry checkpoints there; the election is persisted only at
    89		// the delivery points below, once those checkpoints actually arrived.
    90		// Everything in between can still stop delivery, and the election is
    91		// permanent, so intent is not enough to move it. The hint below then speaks
    92		// only for what capture left gated — see hintGatedCheckpointSync.
    93		var pendingCapture string
    94		if !ps.hasCheckpointURL() {
    95			if pendingCaptureCheckpointSyncRemote(ctx, ps.remote) {
    96				pendingCapture = ps.remote
    97			}
    98			if !checkpointSyncAllowedForRemote(ctx, ps.remote, pendingCapture) {
    99				hintGatedCheckpointSync(ctx, ps.remote)
   100				return nil
   101			}
   102		}
   103	
   104		// git-refs primary: push the per-checkpoint refs recorded in the push queue
   105		// instead of the single v1 branch. Those refs live under refs/entire/, not
   106		// refs/heads/, so a forge can never pick them as a repository's default
   107		// branch — the empty-remote guard below is unnecessary for this backend.
   108		// (A configured git-branch mirror's v1 ref is not pushed here yet — mirror
   109		// push for downgrade safety is a later step.)
   110		if ps.primaryIsRefs {
   111			return s.prePushCheckpointRefs(ctx, ps, pendingCapture)
   112		}
   113	
   114		// git-branch primary: entire/checkpoints/v1 is a real refs/heads branch, so
   115		// on an otherwise-empty remote a forge like GitHub would select it as the
   116		// default. Defer publication until the user's own branch exists there.
   117		deferAutomaticCheckpointPush := protectFirstUserBranch && deferCheckpointPushOnEmptyRemote(ctx, ps)
   118	
   119		refs := checkpoint.ResolveRefs(ctx)
   120		repo, repoErr := OpenRepository(ctx)
   121		if repoErr != nil {
   122			logging.Warn(ctx, "checkpoint policy pre-push: failed to open repository; allowing checkpoint push",
   123				slog.String("error", repoErr.Error()),
   124			)
   125		} else {
   126			defer repo.Close()
   127			syncCheckpointPolicyForPrePush(ctx, repo, ps)
   128			if !checkpointPolicyAllowsGitHook(ctx, repo) {
   129				// Policy failures should skip checkpoint pushes, not abort the user's push.
   130				return nil
   131			}
   132		}
   133	
   134		// OPF pre-push rewrite: if OPF is configured, resolve the user's
   135		// decision (env > settings > prompt > non-TTY auto-run), then
   136		// re-redact unpushed v1 commits with OPF (producing the OPF-applied,
   137		// 9-layer pipeline) before pushing. Skipped entirely when OPF is off,
   138		// so the common-case fast path is unchanged.
   139		if redact.OPFEnabled() {
   140			decision, decisionErr := opfPrePushDecision(ctx)
   141			if decisionErr != nil {
   142				logging.Warn(ctx, "OPF pre-push decision failed; aborting push",
   143					slog.String("error", decisionErr.Error()),
   144				)
   145				return decisionErr
   146			}
   147			switch decision {
   148			case OPFAbort:
   149				return errOPFAbortedByUser
   150			case OPFSkip:
   151				// User opted out for this push (or settings/env say
   152				// "never"). Push regex-only (8-layer) content as-is.
   153				logging.Info(ctx, "OPF skipped for this push (user choice or settings)")
   154			case OPFRun:
   155				_, opfSpan := perf.Start(ctx, "opf_pre_push_rewrite")
   156				if repoErr != nil {
   157					opfSpan.RecordError(repoErr)
   158					opfSpan.End()
   159					logging.Warn(ctx, "OPF pre-push: failed to open repo; aborting push",
   160						slog.String("error", repoErr.Error()),
   161					)
   162					return repoErr
   163				}

   165					opfSpan.RecordError(rewriteErr)
   166					opfSpan.End()
   167					logging.Warn(ctx, "OPF pre-push rewrite failed; aborting push",
   168						slog.String("error", rewriteErr.Error()),
   169					)
   170					return rewriteErr
   171				}
   172				opfSpan.End()
   173			}
   174		}
   175	
   176		if deferAutomaticCheckpointPush {
   177			// Do this only after OPF has had a chance to rewrite v1: the outer
   178			// user push may explicitly include the metadata branch.
   179			logging.Info(ctx, "automatic checkpoint push deferred until the remote has a branch",
   180				slog.String("remote", ps.remote),
   181			)
   182			return nil
   183		}
   184	
   185		// Thread the span's context into the push so the network push and any
   186		// fetch+rebase recovery nest beneath it as child steps in the perf trace.
   187		pushCtx, pushCheckpointsSpan := perf.Start(ctx, "push_checkpoint_refs")
   188		// Capture needs checkpoint data CONFIRMED on this remote, so count what
   189		// landed rather than trusting the absence of an error: every ref that was due
   190		// has to deliver, and at least one has to actually do so. Delivery must come
   191		// from pushRefIfNeeded's delivered return and NOT from err, which is
   192		// fail-soft and nil even when the remote refused the ref.
   193		deliveredCount, anyFailed := 0, false
   194		for _, ref := range refs.Push {
   195			delivered, err := pushRefIfNeeded(pushCtx, ps.pushTarget(), ref)
   196			if err != nil {
   197				pushCheckpointsSpan.RecordError(err)
   198				pushCheckpointsSpan.End()
   199				return err
   200			}
   201			if delivered {
   202				deliveredCount++
   203			} else {
   204				anyFailed = true
   205			}
   206		}
   207		pushCheckpointsSpan.End()
   208	
   209		// Delivered: the election may now follow the push that carried it. A push that
   210		// carried nothing — an empty ref set, or a v1 ref that does not exist locally
   211		// yet — leaves the election alone. It is safe either way (nothing is stranded
   212		// when there was nothing to strand), but capturing would announce a move that
   213		// moved no data, which is the class of claim this whole path exists to stop
   214		// making. The next push that carries a checkpoint captures instead.
   215		if pendingCapture != "" && deliveredCount > 0 && !anyFailed {
   216			commitCapturedSyncRemote(ctx, pendingCapture)
   217		}
   218	
   219		cleanupPushedShadowBranches(ctx)
   220		return nil
   221	}

   235	// opfGateForCheckpointRefs resolves the OPF decision and, when it says run,
   236	// rewrites the queued checkpoint refs. A nil error means the flush may proceed;
   237	// a non-nil one means it must be withheld, leaving the refs queued rather than
   238	// shipping 8-layer content the user did not opt out of.
   239	//
   240	// Every path that flushes the queue must pass through here, because skipping it
   241	// is not the same as an OPFSkip: a skip is a decision the user made for this
   242	// push and it ships untagged content deliberately, while a missing gate ships
   243	// exactly the same bytes having never asked. That is the shape the migration
   244	// command's opt-in push had before this was shared.

   246	// Reporting belongs to the caller: the pre-push hook warns and carries on,

   248	// an explicitly requested push surfaces the error instead.

   252			return err
   253		}

   255		case OPFAbort:
   256			return errOPFAbortedByUser
   257		case OPFSkip:
   258			// Explicit opt-out for this push: flush the 8-layer content as-is,
   259			// untagged — same as the v1 path.
   260			logging.Info(ctx, "OPF skipped for this push (user choice or settings)")

   262			_, opfSpan := perf.Start(ctx, "opf_pre_push_rewrite_refs")

   266				return rewriteErr
   267			}
   268		}
   269		return nil
   270	}

   283	// deferCheckpointPushOnEmptyRemote reports whether publication of the git-branch
   284	// v1 metadata should be held back because the push remote may be brand new.
   285	//
   286	// Hosting providers such as GitHub make the first branch pushed to an empty
   287	// repository its default, so the pre-push hook must not publish
   288	// entire/checkpoints/v1 ahead of the user's own first branch. The check is
   289	// purely local: if a remote-tracking ref for this remote already exists
   290	// (refs/remotes/<remote>/*), the remote has been fetched from or pushed to
   291	// before and therefore already has at least one branch, so publishing cannot
   292	// make our metadata the default. Otherwise defer — git records a
   293	// remote-tracking ref after the first successful push, so the deferred metadata
   294	// publishes on the next push.
   295	//
   296	// It deliberately performs no ls-remote/fetch. A network round trip on the
   297	// pre-push path can trigger an SSH security-key touch prompt (and doing so per
   298	// push URL would multiply those prompts), which is a poor pre-push UX. This is
   299	// also why it uses only the remote git handed the hook rather than resolving
   300	// every configured push URL.
   301	//
   302	// A separate checkpoint remote is exempt: it is a dedicated metadata store, not
   303	// the repository the user pushes to.
   304	func deferCheckpointPushOnEmptyRemote(ctx context.Context, ps pushSettings) bool {
   305		if ps.hasCheckpointURL() {
   306			return false
   307		}
   308	
   309		// The hazard only arises for a configured remote (the `git remote add
   310		// origin …` then first-push flow). Pushing straight to a bare URL hands that
   311		// URL to the hook as the remote arg, and git never records a
   312		// refs/remotes/<url>/* tracking ref for it — so a tracking-ref check would
   313		// defer the metadata forever. Publish for a non-configured (URL) target
   314		// rather than strand it; the first-branch scenario always uses a named
   315		// remote.
   316		if !isConfiguredRemote(ctx, ps.remote) {
   317			return false
   318		}
   319	
   320		// Known limitation, accepted for the no-network design: a tracking ref left
   321		// over from before a remote was deleted and recreated empty under the same
   322		// URL reads as "established", so v1 would publish to the now-empty remote.
   323		// Detecting that requires asking the remote — the network round trip we
   324		// deliberately avoid here. The scenario is rare and its default branch is
   325		// recoverable by resetting it on the forge.
   326		return !remoteHasTrackingRefs(ctx, ps.remote)
   327	}

   329	// isConfiguredRemote reports whether name is a configured git remote, as
   330	// opposed to a bare URL that git passes through verbatim when a push targets a
   331	// URL directly. Local and best-effort (reads config, no network); any error is
   332	// treated as "not a configured remote".
   333	func isConfiguredRemote(ctx context.Context, name string) bool {
   334		if name == "" {
   335			return false
   336		}
   337		return cachedIsConfiguredRemote(ctx, name, func() (bool, error) {
   338			cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, "git", "remote", "get-url", name)
   339			if worktreeRoot, ok := settings.WorktreeRoot(ctx); ok {
   340				cmd.Dir = worktreeRoot
   341			}
   342			err := cmd.Run()
   343			if err == nil {
   344				return true, nil
   345			}
   346			// git ran and said no: a real answer worth caching. git failing to run at
   347			// all says nothing about the remote, and memoizing that false would
   348			// fail-close checkpoint_push_remote for the rest of the process.
   349			var exitErr *exec.ExitError
   350			if errors.As(err, &exitErr) {
   351				return false, nil
   352			}
   353			return false, fmt.Errorf("probe remote %q: %w", name, err)
   354		})

   358	// locally. Its presence means the remote has been fetched from or pushed to
   359	// before and so already has at least one branch. Local-only and best-effort:

   369		}
   370		return strings.TrimSpace(string(out)) != ""

   373	// prePushCheckpointRefs drains the per-checkpoint push queue and batch-pushes the
   374	// recorded refs fast-forward-only (git-refs primary; never a force push — a
   375	// diverged ref is recovered via fetch+replay). Transient push failures are logged and

   377	// refs stay queued for the next pre-push. When OPF is enabled the queued refs
   378	// are re-redacted with it first (RewriteQueuedCheckpointRefsWithOPF).

   382	// local format), which is independent of the storage backend, so a blocked
   383	// policy skips the ref push (leaving refs queued) rather than pushing.

   388				slog.String("error", err.Error()))

   390		}
   391		defer repo.Close()

   393		// Refresh the checkpoint policy from the remote, then skip the ref push
   394		// (leaving refs queued) if the policy is diverged or the local format is
   395		// unsupported — same gate the v1 path uses.
   396		syncCheckpointPolicyForPrePush(ctx, repo, ps)
   397		if !checkpointPolicyAllowsGitHook(ctx, repo) {
   398			return nil
   399		}
   400	
   401		// OPF backend divergence: both paths fail closed, but this one does it
   402		// without blocking the user. The v1 path aborts the user's git push; here a
   403		// checkpoint-ref failure must never do that (see this function's doc), so
   404		// failing closed means withholding the flush — nothing un-OPF'd ships, the
   405		// refs stay queued, and the user's push proceeds.
   406		if redact.OPFEnabled() {
   407			if opfErr := opfGateForCheckpointRefs(ctx, repo); opfErr != nil {
   408				warnOPFCheckpointRefsWithheld(ctx, opfErr)
   409				return nil
   410			}
   411		}
   412	
   413		if flushed, err := flushCheckpointRefsQueue(ctx, repo, ps); err == nil {

   415			// nothing, so it must not move the election or announce that it had.
   416			if pendingCapture != "" && flushed > 0 {
   417				commitCapturedSyncRemote(ctx, pendingCapture)
   418			}
   419		} else {
   420			// Fail-soft: a checkpoint-ref push failure must never block the user's
   421			// git push. The refs stay queued for the next pre-push.
   422			logging.Warn(ctx, "git-refs pre-push: checkpoint ref push failed; refs left queued",
   423				slog.String("error", err.Error()))
   424		}
   425	
   426		cleanupPushedShadowBranches(ctx)
   427		return nil
   428	}

   430	// PushQueuedCheckpointRefs pushes any queued checkpoint refs to the configured
   431	// checkpoint remote, surfacing errors (unlike the fail-soft pre-push path); the
   432	// caller owns the repo. It returns the number of refs pushed and whether
   433	// pushing is disabled in settings — a distinct signal from pushed==0 with
   434	// pushing enabled (an empty queue), so callers can report the two accurately.
   435	// Like the pre-push paths, a checkpoint policy that blocks pushing — or, when
   436	// OPF is enabled, an OPF rewrite that cannot run — errors with the refs left
   437	// queued. Currently used by the checkpoint migration command's opt-in
   438	// "push now".
   439	func PushQueuedCheckpointRefs(ctx context.Context, repo *git.Repository, remote string) (pushed int, pushDisabled bool, err error) {
   440		ps := resolvePushSettings(ctx, remote)
   441		if ps.pushDisabled {
   442			return 0, true, nil
   443		}
   444		syncCheckpointPolicyForPrePush(ctx, repo, ps)
   445		if !checkpointPolicyAllowsGitHook(ctx, repo) {
   446			return 0, false, errors.New("checkpoint policy does not allow pushing checkpoint refs; refs stay queued")
   447		}
   448		// The same OPF gate the pre-push path applies, in the same position, for
   449		// the same reason: nothing un-OPF'd may leave the machine. Only the failure
   450		// direction differs. Pre-push withholds silently so the user's git push is
   451		// never blocked; this push was explicitly asked for, so it fails loudly with
   452		// the refs left queued — matching the checkpoint-policy branch above, and
   453		// leaving the next `git push` to apply OPF and deliver them.
   454		if redact.OPFEnabled() {
   455			if opfErr := opfGateForCheckpointRefs(ctx, repo); opfErr != nil {
   456				return 0, false, fmt.Errorf("OPF did not run, so checkpoint refs stay queued: %w", opfErr)
   457			}
   458		}
   459		pushed, err = flushCheckpointRefsQueue(ctx, repo, ps)
   460		// Clean up even on a partial/failed flush: a diverged batch can push some
   461		// refs and still return an error, and the shadow branches for the refs that
   462		// *did* land must still be cleaned up — parity with the pre-push path, which
   463		// always runs cleanup after flush regardless of its error.
   464		cleanupPushedShadowBranches(ctx)
   465		return pushed, false, err

   468	// flushCheckpointRefsQueue drains the push-discovery queue and batch-pushes the
   469	// recorded refs fast-forward-only, recovering a diverged ref by fetch+replay and
   470	// removing from the queue only the refs that land. It returns the number pushed.
   471	//
   472	// Shared by the git-refs pre-push path (which logs and ignores the error to
   473	// never block the user's push) and the migration command's opt-in push (which
   474	// surfaces it). Stale entries — refs no longer present locally — are pruned so
   475	// they don't block the queue forever.
   476	func flushCheckpointRefsQueue(ctx context.Context, repo *git.Repository, ps pushSettings) (int, error) {
   477		queue, err := checkpoint.PushQueueForRepo(ctx, repo)
   478		if err != nil {
   479			return 0, fmt.Errorf("resolve push queue: %w", err)
   480		}
   481		queued, err := queue.Drain()
   482		if err != nil {
   483			return 0, fmt.Errorf("drain push queue: %w", err)
   484		}
   485		if len(queued) == 0 {
   486			return 0, nil
   487		}
   488	
   489		pushCtx, pushSpan := perf.Start(ctx, "push_checkpoint_refs")
   490		defer pushSpan.End()
   491	
   492		existing, stale := partitionLocalRefs(repo, queued)
   493		if len(stale) > 0 {
   494			if err := queue.Remove(stale); err != nil {
   495				logging.Warn(ctx, "git-refs push: prune stale queue entries failed",
   496					slog.String("error", err.Error()))
   497			}
   498		}
   499		if len(existing) == 0 {
   500			return 0, nil
   501		}
   502	
   503		// Resolved here, not by the caller: it spawns `git remote get-url` and its
   504		// result is unused unless refs are actually pushed, so an ordinary push with
   505		// an empty queue must not pay for it — nor print the multi-URL warning.
   506		dest := resolveRefsPushDestination(pushCtx, ps)

content.text: I have the full picture. Let me confirm one detail about the migrate path's TTY guarantee.

## Altitude review: OPF gate for the checkpoint-ref push queue

**Verdict: the fix is correct but one level too shallow.** It closes the specific hole and it correctly extracts the shared gate, so it is not a bandaid in the "papered over" sense. But it leaves the invariant ("nothing un-OPF'd leaves the queue") as a *convention two callers must remember* rather than a property of the code that owns the queue — and the one-level-deeper version is cheap, feasible, and fixes a second defect for free.

---

### 1. `manual_commit_push.go:406-411, 454-458` — the gate is at both call sites of `flushCheckpointRefsQueue`, not inside it; move it inside with a required failure-policy argument

`flushCheckpointRefsQueue` (line 476) already takes exactly what the gate needs — `(ctx, repo, ps)`, with `repo` used on the very next line — so moving the gate to the top of that function is a no-op signature-wise. The only real objection is the one the diff's own comments raise: the two callers need opposite failure behaviour. That is an argument for a **parameter**, not for two call-site checks.

**Recommendation:** `flushCheckpointRefsQueue(ctx, repo, ps, opfPolicy)` where `opfPolicy` is an unexported enum with two values (`opfWithholdQuietly` for pre-push, `opfSurfaceError` for the migrate path). The gate runs inside; on failure the function either warns via `warnOPFCheckpointRefsWithheld` and returns `(0, nil)`, or returns `(0, wrappedErr)`. A future third caller **cannot compile** without stating its policy, which is strictly stronger than any comment or guard test.

Two behavioural deltas to accept deliberately, both benign:
- Pre-push currently returns early on withhold and so skips `cleanupPushedShadowBranches` (line 426). Inside-flush, cleanup would run — harmless, since it only deletes shadow branches for refs already delivered.
- `pendingCapture` is already keyed on `flushed > 0` (line 416), so a withheld flush returning `0` naturally declines to move the election. No change needed.

**Tradeoff:** `flushCheckpointRefsQueue` gains one knob and a `redact` dependency it does not have today. In exchange, the queue's own function owns its egress invariant instead of two (later N) callers.

---

### 2. `manual_commit_push.go:454` — the gate resolves the OPF *decision* above the empty-queue check, so the diff propagates a prompt-with-nothing-to-push into a new, interactive command

`opfGateForCheckpointRefs` calls `opfPrePushDecision` → `askOPFPrompt` (a `huh` form) **before** anything knows whether the queue has entries; `flushCheckpointRefsQueue` returns `0` on an empty queue (line 485), and `RewriteQueuedCheckpointRefsWithOPF` peeks and returns nil (opf_refs.go:45). `doctor_migrate.go:110` gates the whole push-now path on `CanPromptInteractively()`, so a TTY is guaranteed there — meaning with OPF enabled and no persisted `prompt_default`, the user is now asked *"Run OpenAI Privacy Filter on these checkpoints? Adds ~30s"*, answers yes, and gets `"No queued refs to push (they may have already been pushed)."` — the exact race `doctor_migrate.go:113-115` documents. On the pre-push side the same misplacement prints the `→ OpenAI Privacy Filter: scanning… (~30s)` line on every non-TTY push with an empty queue.

This is the concrete payoff of finding 1, not a separate fix: put the gate after `flushCheckpointRefsQueue`'s `len(queued) == 0` / `len(existing) == 0` early returns (lines 485, 499) and the class disappears for both callers at once.

**One tension to resolve explicitly, not silently:** `OPFNoCategoriesError`'s doc (opf_rewrite.go:~230) states the v1 decision gate runs "with no knowledge of whether anything is unpushed, so a misconfigured repo aborts every push — including one with nothing to rewrite." Moving the decision below the empty check gives up that for the refs backend. **Take that trade** — a push that ships nothing cannot ship unscanned content, and the fail-closed no-categories check is already independently enforced inside the rewrite at `opf_refs.go:52`. Say so in the doc rather than leaving the two backends' stated rationales contradicting each other.

---

### 3. `push_common.go:58` and `:168` — a genuine cross-backend chokepoint exists, and the invariant worth enforcing there is a *postcondition on the trailer*, not "was the gate called"

Both backends converge: git-refs goes `flushCheckpointRefsQueue` → `batchPushRefs` (push_common.go:58); git-branch goes `prePush` → `pushRefIfNeeded` → `doPushRef` → `tryPushRefCommon` (push_common.go:168, 364) → `remote.Push`. Both bottom out in `checkpoint/remote.PushWithOptions` (git.go:428). So the egress is single, but `PushWithOptions` is the wrong altitude for the check: it has no repo handle, no notion of the decision, and it also carries the checkpoint-*policy* ref, which is not checkpoint content. `push_common.go` is the right one — both functions live in that one file and are the only two ways checkpoint content leaves.

The check that belongs there is not "did someone call a gate" but the property the gate is supposed to produce, which the data already self-describes: every commit OPF has processed carries `Entire-OPF-Applied: true`, and `trailers.HasOPFApplied` already serves as the watermark in `unappliedAncestry` (opf_refs.go:192). So: `assertOPFAppliedIfRequired(ctx, repo, refs)` — when `redact.OPFEnabled()` and this process did not record an explicit `OPFSkip`, refuse to push a checkpoint ref whose tip lacks the trailer. One commit-object read per ref, negligible next to a network round-trip, and backend-agnostic by construction.

**Recommendation:** do finding 1 now (small, closes the refs backend); file the egress assertion as the follow-up that closes it for both. **Tradeoff:** the assertion needs a memoized per-process decision so an intentional `OPFSkip` is distinguishable from a missing gate — that plumbing is the real cost, and it is why this is a follow-up and not a blocker on this diff.

Note the asymmetry the diff creates in the meantime: the refs backend now has a named, documented gate whose comment says *"Every path that flushes the queue must pass through here"*, while the v1 backend's identical logic is still 35 lines inline in `prePush` (lines 139-174). Either extract the symmetric `opfGateForV1` or say in the doc that v1 keeps its own copy — as written, a reader can reasonably read `opfGateForCheckpointRefs` as *the* OPF gate.

---

### 4. `manual_commit_push.go:246-248` — the asymmetric failure behaviour lives in prose in a doc comment, one level away from the two branches that implement it

The gate's doc says *"Reporting belongs to the caller: the pre-push hook warns and carries on… while an explicitly requested push surfaces the error instead."* Nothing in any signature or type says that. A future reader has to hold three files open — the gate's doc (246), the pre-push caller's `return nil` (409), and the migrate caller's `fmt.Errorf` (456) — and reconstruct that the difference is intended rather than an oversight. That is precisely the reconstruction the original bug represents: someone read `PushQueuedCheckpointRefs` and did not reconstruct that a gate was owed at all.

**Recommendation:** name the two behaviours as the policy values from finding 1 (`opfWithholdQuietly` / `opfSurfaceError`), each with a one-line doc carrying the *reason* ("a checkpoint failure must never block the user's git push" / "this push was explicitly requested"). The asymmetry then appears at the call site as a word the reader can look up, and the prose in the gate's doc shrinks to a pointer. **Tradeoff:** two more identifiers; in exchange the invariant and its two sanctioned failure directions are stated once, in the type, where they cannot drift apart.

---

### 5. Guard test: **not warranted here** — the repo's guard-test precedent exists for constraints the type system cannot express, and this one it can

`TestGitStatusCallSitesPassNoOptionalLocks` (gitrepo/gitstatus_guard_test.go), `TestRootBasesAreTrusted` (osroot/rootbase_guard_test.go), and `TestEntireDirCheckExemptions` all guard things a signature cannot: a string flag buried in a variadic argv, an allowlist of files permitted to call a constructor, a set of annotations. A "did you call the gate" grep-guard for `flushCheckpointRefsQueue` would be strictly weaker than the required parameter in finding 1 — it fails after the fact instead of at compile time, it needs its own staleness detector (the `checked == 0` bail-out), and it would be defeated by any caller that wraps the flush in a helper.

If a source-level guard is wanted anyway, the practical shape is not "callers pass through the gate" but the finding-3 property expressed as a **behavioural** test in `refs_push_test.go`, alongside the two the diff already adds: a table over every exported entry point that can push checkpoint content (`PrePush`, `PrePushFromGitHook`, `PushQueuedCheckpointRefs`) asserting that with OPF enabled and a failing OPF the remote receives nothing, and with a working OPF everything on the remote carries the trailer. Adding an entry point without a row is visible in review in a way an omitted call-site check is not; and unlike a grep-guard it survives refactoring the internals. **Tradeoff:** it costs a real git fixture per row (the diff's two new tests already pay that), versus a grep-guard's near-zero runtime and near-zero value here.

---

### What the diff gets right, so it is not re-litigated

The extraction itself is the correct decomposition: error-returning gate, reporting owned by the caller, `OPFSkip` deliberately falling through with the "not the same as a missing gate" distinction spelled out (lines 240-244) — that comment names the actual bug class rather than restating the code. The two new tests test the *observable property* (what reached the bare remote, what stayed queued) rather than that a function was called, which is why they will survive the deeper refactor above unchanged.
